title: Logarithmic Scales
short: Each step on a log scale multiplies by the same factor, as in decibels and pH.
trouble: Students think a pH of 4 is twice as acidic as a pH of 8, when it is ten thousand times as acidic.

blocks.html: When quantities range from tiny to huge, scientists measure them on a scale of exponents, a logarithmic scale. You already read log graphs; now you read log scales.

On a log scale, each step of 1 means multiplying by the base (usually 10). pH: $\text{pH} = -\log[H^+]$, so one pH unit is a factor of 10 in acidity. Decibels: $L = 10\log\frac{I}{I_0}$, so 10 dB is a factor of 10 in intensity. A difference of $d$ on the scale means a ratio of $10^d$ (for decibels, $10^{d/10}$).

The log of a product is a sum, so multiplying a quantity by 10 adds 1 to its log. That turns a range like $10^{-14}$ to $1$ into a tidy scale from 14 to 0. The price is that the scale does not add up the way it looks: going from pH 4 to pH 2 is not "twice as acidic," it is $10^2 = 100$ times.

blocks.cap: Drag the number on the bottom line. On the log line, 2, 20, 200 and 2000 are evenly spaced: each step multiplies by 10.

blocks.title: Acidity
blocks.q: How many times more acidic is pH 4 than pH 8?

blocks.title: Loudness
blocks.q: A sound is 30 dB louder than another. How many times greater is its intensity?

blocks.html: Reading a log scale as if it were linear. A pH of 4 is not "twice as acidic" as a pH of 8. The difference is 4 units, and each unit is a factor of 10, so it is $10^4 = 10{,}000$ times as acidic. Subtract the scale values, then raise 10 to that power.
